prehistoric: The oldest human footprints discovered in Europe are approximately 850,000 years old, found at Happisburgh in Norfolk, UK.
The Lascaux cave paintings in France were discovered by four teenagers who were following their dog when it fell into a hole leading to the cave.
The earliest known musical instruments are flutes made from bird bone and mammoth ivory, dating back 42,000 to 43,000 years ago.

Modern humans (Homo sapiens) and Neanderthals overlapped in Europe for roughly 2,600 to 5,400 years, and DNA shows they interbred, so most people outside Africa carry a small share of Neanderthal DNA.
preCataclysm: The Sphinx in Egypt shows evidence of water erosion that some geologists argue could only have occurred much earlier than its conventional dating, possibly during the rainy period at the end of the last ice age.

Similar architectural techniques for fitting massive stone blocks together with incredible precision can be found in ancient sites across the world, from Peru to Egypt, despite no known contact between these civilizations.
Many ancient sites around the world are aligned with astronomical events and constellations, showing a sophistication in astronomy that is easy to underestimate.

Hundreds of ancient flood myths from different cultures around the world share striking similarities, potentially suggesting a common origin from a real catastrophic event. One candidate: as the Ice Age ended, the oceans rose about 120 meters, drowning coastlines worldwide, from Australia to the Persian Gulf.
cataclysm: A thin black layer of soil called the 'black mat' can be found at dozens of sites across North America dating to about 12,900 years ago, containing unusual materials including nanodiamonds, which some scientists believe were created by a cosmic impact.
About 35 genera of large mammals in North America, including mammoths and giant ground sloths, died out around the time of the Younger Dryas cooling period.
Ice core samples from Greenland show that temperatures there dropped by roughly 4 to 10°C (7 to 18°F) as the Younger Dryas set in, and parts of the climate system flipped within just a few years.

Extensive evidence of massive flooding exists throughout Washington state in the 'Channeled Scablands', created when ice dams holding glacial Lake Missoula repeatedly failed between about 18,000 and 15,000 years ago.
recovery: The end of the Younger Dryas period around 11,700 years ago saw Greenland temperatures climb steeply over about 50 years, with some ice-core signals flipping within 1 to 3 years.

The 12,000-year-old temple complex at Göbekli Tepe in Turkey was filled in around 8000 BCE, which its excavator Klaus Schmidt read as deliberate burial, and lay hidden until Schmidt recognised it in 1994.
Many indigenous cultures preserved knowledge through oral traditions that were later dismissed as 'myths' but have sometimes been verified by modern archaeology.

Ancient measuring systems from different cultures often share mathematical relationships. Most researchers trace this to units based on the human body, like the foot and the cubit; others suspect a common, earlier system of measurement.
prePotteryNeolithic: At Göbekli Tepe, the massive T-shaped pillars, weighing around 10 tons each for the tallest, were carved and moved without the use of metal tools or even pottery, as neither was in use in the region yet.
The ancient city of Jericho has been settled, on and off, for over 11,000 years, making it one of the oldest settled places in the world.
Evidence suggests that dogs were the first animals domesticated by humans, possibly as early as 30,000 years ago, long before other animals or plants.
Early farmers in the Fertile Crescent selected wheat plants with non-shattering seed heads, an evolutionary disadvantage in the wild but perfect for human harvesting.
potteryNeolithic: At Çatalhöyük, residents buried their dead beneath the floors of their houses, sometimes repeatedly excavating and reburying the remains.
The earliest known pottery, made in East Asia more than 15,000 years ago, was used for cooking. Food residues on Japanese Jomon pots show that fish and shellfish were boiled in them.
The spread of agriculture into Europe followed two main routes: the Mediterranean coast and the Danube River valley.
Early Neolithic farmers were significantly shorter and experienced more dental problems than their hunter-gatherer counterparts, suggesting agriculture initially led to a decline in health.
chalcolithic: The Iceman 'Ötzi', who lived around 3300 BCE, had 61 tattoos made by rubbing charcoal into small cuts in the skin, possibly for therapeutic purposes.
The oldest known wheel used for transportation was found in Slovenia and dates to around 3200 BCE.
Early copper smelting reached temperatures of over 1,000°C (1,832°F), requiring sophisticated furnace technology and understanding of air flow.
One of the earliest known systems of writing (proto-cuneiform) was not created to record stories or ideas, but to keep track of economic transactions and property.
bronzeAge: The Great Pyramid of Giza is aligned to true north with an error of only about 3/60th of a degree, an impressive result for builders without modern instruments.
One of the oldest surviving toothpaste recipes is on an Egyptian papyrus from about the 4th century CE. It called for rock salt, mint, dried iris flower and grains of pepper, ground together.
Some of the stone blocks in the Great Pyramid weigh up to 80 tons and were transported from quarries more than 500 miles away.
The Bronze Age collapse around 1200 BCE saw many major cities in the eastern Mediterranean destroyed or abandoned within about 50 years, for reasons still debated.
classical: Ancient Rome had apartment buildings called 'insulae' that were commonly five or six stories high, and some may have been taller before emperors limited their height to about 70 Roman feet.
The ancient Greeks had a working steam engine called the aeolipile, invented by Hero of Alexandria around 60 CE, but it was used only as a toy and demonstration device.
Many Ming-era Chinese walls, including some sections of the Great Wall, used a mortar made with sticky rice, which helped make them strong and durable.
The Antikythera Mechanism, discovered in a shipwreck from around 60 BCE, is an ancient Greek analog computer used to predict astronomical positions and eclipses decades in advance.
postClassical: During the Islamic Golden Age (8th to 14th centuries), medieval accounts say the city of Cordoba in Spain had 70 libraries, and that the library of caliph al-Hakam II held some 400,000 books. Historians think these numbers are exaggerated, but they were far larger than anything in Christian Europe, where even large libraries held only a few hundred manuscripts.

The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan had a population of around 200,000 people in the early 16th century, making it one of the largest cities in the world at that time, comparable to Paris and Naples and larger than most European cities.

Some researchers think Viking navigators may have used 'sunstones' (crystals of Icelandic spar) to find the sun's position on cloudy days by polarizing the light. This is a hypothesis: the sagas mention a 'sunstone' only briefly, and no such crystal has been clearly identified at a Viking site.
The Angkor Wat temple complex in Cambodia is the largest religious monument in the world, covering an area of approximately 400 acres.
earlyModern: Christopher Columbus never reached what is now the United States or Canada. His four voyages took him to Caribbean islands and the coasts of Central and South America.
The first newspaper published in North America, 'Publick Occurrences Both Forreign and Domestick', was shut down after just one issue in 1690 because it published without authority.
Isaac Newton wrote more about alchemy and theology than about mathematics and physics. His surviving papers include roughly a million words on alchemy alone.
The Salem Witch Trials in 1692-93 led to the execution of 20 people, but none of them were actually burned at the stake—19 were hanged and one was pressed to death with heavy stones.
modern: Ada Lovelace published what is often called the first computer program, an algorithm for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, in 1843, over a century before modern computers were built.
The 1918 influenza pandemic infected about 500 million people, or one-third of the world's population at the time, and killed at least 50 million, with some estimates as high as 100 million.
The shortest war in recorded history was the Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896, which lasted just 38 minutes from declaration to surrender.
During World War II, the Oscar statuettes were made of painted plaster instead of gold-plated bronze due to metal shortages. Winners later received the proper statues after the war ended.
